newsitem.title: EGYPT: Netanyahu ensures hostile reception in Cairo.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu ensures hostile reception in Cairo.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ensured a hostile reception when he visits Egypt for talks with President Hosni Mubarak on Wednesday by ordering four Palestinian offices in Arab East Jerusalem to close.

The decision on Tuesday evening came too late for Egypt to react but it is bound to reinforce suspicions in Cairo that the right-wing Israeli leader is bent on confrontation with Egypt's Palestinian friends and allies.
The visit, Netanyahu's second to Cairo since he took office in June, was already under a cloud because of Israeli plans to build more houses for Jews in the disputed part of Jerusalem.

"Netanyahu's policies have convinced the Egyptian people and the Arab peoples that Israel is proceeding in the peace process against its will," said an editorial in Wednesday's edition of the government newspaper al-Akhbar.
"How can we Arabs deal with trust and in a normal manner with such people, who smile and laugh whenever peace runs into a crisis?" it added.
Broad sectors of Egyptian public opinion oppose the very concept of a visit by Netanyahu and al-Akhbar said even those in government would look askance at his presence.

"Would it not be better for Mr Netanyahu to feel that Egyptians are welcoming him...instead of seeing angry looks in the eyes of all, even if they have to accept his presence merely as an official guest?" it asked.

Mubarak has repeatedly told Netanyahu his policies -- settling Jews in Palestinian areas and refusing to give the Golan Heights back to Syria -- are undoing the progress made towards peace in the Middle East. He says the outcome could be outbreaks of violence by angry Palestinians.

But the Egyptian president, whose country was the first in the Arab world to make peace with the Jewish state, has so far held at bay those who call for dramatic gestures such as cutting contacts with Israelis.
Questioned on Netanyahu's visit on Monday, Mubarak said Egyptian policy was to keep talking and he would tell Netanyahu of the repercussions of Israeli policy.
The visit is part of a flurry of high-level diplomatic activity focused on Israel's plans for Jerusalem.

Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat is in the United States and will pass through Cairo on his way home, just in time to brief Mubarak in time for Mubarak's own talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Washington next week.
Kings Hussein of Jordan and Hassan of Morocco are also expected to see Clinton later this month.
The U.N. Security Council had planned to discuss the Jerusalem housing project on Tuesday but it postponed the meeting until Wednesday at the request of the United States.
Arafat, who consults frequently with Mubarak on his talks with the Israelis, has also tried to avert a crisis.
He said in Washington on Tuesday that he had no alternative but to treat Netanyahu as a "partner" in peace talks.
